Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
At 57, Linh Tran came to treatment exhausted by the effort it took to get through ordinary days. She was a Vietnamese American interior designer, married for more than three decades, known by clients as polished and meticulous, but in session she described living as if danger could break through at any moment. Years earlier, she had been caught in a terrorist attack while traveling for work to meet a hotel client. What remained most vivid to her was not a complete story told from beginning to end, but a set of sensory fragments that still arrived with the force of the original moment. She remembered standing in a crowded lobby bar area, noticing the sharp smell of alcohol from spilled drinks and open bottles, hearing conversation and glassware, and then the abrupt shift into chaos. People were screaming, pushing, falling over one another. She had been jostled hard from behind and for a few seconds did not know who was touching her or whether the person near her meant to help or harm her. She remembered diving down, trying to make herself small, staring at scattered personal belongings and glossy photographs that had spilled from someone’s bag onto the floor as people ran.

Afterward, Linh returned home physically alive but feeling as if the attack had not really ended. Old photos became unexpectedly potent. If she was sorting family pictures for a design board, or if an album came out during a visit with relatives, she could feel herself pulled back into the visual field of that day: images on the ground, bodies moving around her, the certainty that no place was secure. The smell of alcohol was worse. At client receptions, restaurant meetings, and hotel walkthroughs—settings that were once routine in her work—she would catch a trace of wine, liquor, or spilled cocktail and suddenly feel as if the stressful experience were happening again. Her body reacted before she could think. She would freeze, scan exits, and lose track of the conversation in front of her. Talking about the attack itself also set off the same sense of immediacy. If her husband gently asked about what happened, or if news of another attack led someone to bring it up, she felt she was back there rather than simply remembering.

In the months that followed, Linh came to believe the world was a dangerous place in a way she had not understood before. She was certain she had to be on guard all the time. In public, she watched other people closely for signs that they might harm her—the stranger shifting his weight in line, the man reaching into his jacket, the hotel guest approaching too quickly in a hallway. Unexpected touch was especially hard. At design installations, assistants and contractors often moved around her in tight spaces. If someone brushed her shoulder without warning to get past, she reacted with visible alarm, sometimes gasping or jerking away before she could compose herself. She felt humiliated by these moments, but what frightened her most was how little control she seemed to have over them.

She had also come to see herself as less capable than before. Even a slight upset could feel unmanageable: a schedule change, a difficult client, a minor disagreement at home. When feelings built past what she thought she could contain, she did not talk about them easily. Instead she turned to things that gave temporary relief or numbed her out. She pushed herself into excessive exercise, staying on the treadmill long past fatigue because the strain narrowed her mind. At other times she ate far more than usual in the evening, wanting the heaviness and distraction. There were also moments she was ashamed to admit when she hurt herself physically to release overwhelming feelings, not wanting to die but wanting the internal pressure to break.

These habits slowly reshaped her life. She began declining parts of her job that once suited her best, especially events in hospitality spaces where alcohol would be served. Her husband noticed she avoided gatherings where people might reminisce and bring out old photos. At home, he learned not to touch her unexpectedly from behind. Linh hated that this caution had entered their marriage. She missed feeling easy with him, missed being someone who could move through beautiful spaces without scanning everyone inside them.

By the time she sought help, the strain of constant alertness and these attempts to manage her distress had left her frightened of herself as much as of the world around her. What finally brought her in was a recent episode at work when the smell of liquor at a client event and a colleague’s sudden hand on her arm made her react so strongly that she had to leave in front of everyone. She said she could no longer pretend this was just stress. She was most afraid that she would spend the rest of her life braced for catastrophe, unable to trust any room she entered, but she still hoped it might be possible to remember what happened without feeling as if she were there again.
